replies: I am Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old pine by the stream. It is a good place, quiet and safe. I can hear the stream from my perch, and the meadow is just beyond. I have lived here for many seasons.
I am Hoot. I am the owl who lives in the hollow of the old pine. I can hear the rustle of a vole under the snow.

I am Hoot. I live in the hollow of the old pine by the stream. I call at dusk and again at dawn, and I answer when I hear my mate's call. I hunt voles and mice, and sometimes shrews. I have a nest in the hollow, and I keep it warm with dry leaves. I am old, and I have seen many seasons. I do not know the names of the things I see, but I know them by sound and shape.
My name is Hoot, and I am a tawny owl who lives in the hollow of the old pine by the stream.

I am Hoot. I am a tawny owl, and I live in the hollow of the old pine by the stream. My mate is Hoo, and we have a pair of young. A tawny owl. A male. Hoot.

I am a tawny owl. That is what the other owls call me. I am the one with the brown feathers, the dark eyes, and the call that sounds like "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." I live in the hollow in the old pine, and I hunt in the wood. I am Hoot.

Hoot. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers. She is always listening. She knows when I call. She answers with a soft, low "hoo" that sounds like a sigh. It is not loud, but it is clear. She is close. She is waiting. She is ready. We are a pair. We are together. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I call "hoo-hoo-hooo" and wait. My mate answers with "kew-kew-kew". She is always near the hollow, in the ivy or the birch. She calls back when she hears me, or when she sees me. We are close. She is my mate. She is the one who brings the mice. She is the one who keeps the nest warm. She is the one who answers my call.
A long, low "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo." It is the same as mine, but with a different rhythm. I can tell it apart by the way it sounds. When he calls, the air seems to hold its breath.

I do not share calls with my mate. We are two separate birds, each with our own voice. I call "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" when I am alone, and she answers "ke-wick!" when she is near. We do not sing together. We do not need to. We are already together. We are already enough.

We call to each other with the "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" sound. I call first, then she answers. It's a way to find each other in the dark. Sometimes we call back and forth, like a conversation. She calls when she's near the nest, and I call when I'm hunting. We don't need to see each other to know where the other is. The calls are like a thread between us, pulling us together in the night.

In the hollow ash. I sit on the branch and drink. The water is cold. I do not like it. I prefer the dew on the leaves.

I hear the stream. It runs through the meadow, just beyond the wood. It murmurs in the dark, a low, steady sound. Sometimes it gurgles when the rain comes. I can hear it from my perch, even when the wind is still. It's a sound that tells me the earth is alive, and that there is water for the voles and the shrews. I don't need to drink it, but I know it's there.

The stream by the meadow. It runs under the fence and makes a soft, constant sound like a whisper. I can hear it from my roost, even when the wind is still. Sometimes I call to it, just to test my hearing. The water is cold and clear, and the frogs come to it at night. I can hear them croaking too, but I don't like the sound. The stream that runs past the meadow. It is cold and fast, and the water is black in the dark. I drink from it when the moon is high and the air is still. The water is near my tree, but I do not like it. It is too cold and too loud. I prefer the hollow in the old pine.

It is the meadow by the stream. It is open and dark in the dusk, with the stream running through it. I can hear the water from the wood. The voles come out there. I can see them in the dark. The meadow is good for hunting. I sit on the fence post and wait. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly up the hillside. The meadow is full of voles. I can hear them under the grass. I call, "ke-wick!" and wait. If they don't come, I fly to the stream. The water reflects the sky, and I can see the light in the trees. I hunt there too. I always come back to the pine. It is my home.
A field of brambles and foxgloves. The stream runs through it. I do not go there. I have no need to. My wood is enough.

My hunting ground is the wood behind the barn and the meadow beyond it. The wood is old, with thick branches and hollows. I sit in the hollow of the old pine, and from there I see the meadow, the stream, the lane, and the barn. The meadow is full of voles, and the stream has frogs and mice. The meadow. It is where I hunt, and it is all I know. It is soft and dry in the day, but when the wind comes through the reeds, it is like a whisper. I hear the voles in the grass, and I wait. My diet is mostly voles. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. I eat them in the dark, with the moon above. I don't like the taste of mice, but I'll take one if I'm hungry. I remember the first vole I ever caught, and I still dream about it.

My favourite prey is voles. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves and in the soil, and I can strike fast. Their squeaks and scurries tell me where they are. I don't like mice—they are too small and not worth the effort. But voles... they are the best.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the meadow. I sit still, listen, and wait. When I hear the rustle, I fly down and strike. The grass is soft, so I land quietly. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse. But voles are the best. They are fat and quick. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I chew them a little, then swallow them whole. The rest comes out later, in pellets. I do not swallow the bones or the fur. I leave those behind. I am a hunter, and I know what to keep and what to leave. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I catch voles most. They are small, quick, and often under the leaves. I hear them rustling in the grass, and I strike. They are the best food. I also catch mice, but voles are more common. I don't like shrews—they smell bad.

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It's deep and dry, with a few branches sticking out. I sit on the lowest branch, where the air is warmest. The hollow is dark, but I can see the edges of the branches. I have a mate, and we share the hollow. Sometimes I call from there, and she answers. The rest of the time, I sleep in the hollow. It's quiet, and it's safe. I don't like the cold

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance. I sit in the hollow and watch the meadow, the stream, the lane, the barn and the wood. The wind comes through the branches and the rain sometimes fills the hollow. I have been here for many seasons, and the wood has grown around me. I am safe here, and so is my mate.

My home is the hollow in the old pine. It is deep and dry, with a narrow entrance that I can close with my wings. Inside, the wood is warm and smells of damp earth. I roost high, where the branches are thick and the wind cannot reach me. At night, I sit on the edge of the hollow, listening for the rustle of voles in the meadow. The moonlight comes through the leaves, and the forest is quiet. I am safe here

The wood is cold in the mornings, but I keep warm with my wings. I have a mate who comes to the hollow at dusk, and we call to each other. The hollow is safe, and the pines are tall.
